subject: ent
title: Nasopharyngeal tumours

steps.tx: **Nasopharyngeal carcinoma** arises most often in the **fossa of Rosenmuller**, just behind the Eustachian tube opening, and it is strongly linked to **Epstein-Barr virus** infection. It is endemic in southern Chinese and Southeast Asian populations, where genetic susceptibility and salted fish nitrosamines add risk. The tumour spreads early to retropharyngeal and level II or level V nodes, so a painless neck lump is often the first sign while the primary stays silent. Non keratinising tumours are virus driven, while keratinising tumours follow smoking and alcohol exposure.
steps.say: The commonest site for this cancer is a small recess behind the opening of the Eustachian tube. Infection with Epstein Barr virus causes most endemic cases in southern China and Southeast Asia. Salted fish and inherited susceptibility further increase the risk in these populations. Spread to the upper neck nodes occurs early, so patients often notice a painless lump first. The original growth usually remains hidden and produces no early warning symptoms.

vis.alt: Diagram illustrating nasopharyngeal carcinoma arising in fossa of Rosenmuller and spreading to neck lymph nodes.
vis.caption: NPC origin and early lymphatic spread

steps.tx: Unilateral **serous otitis media** in an adult is a red flag, because tumour at the tube opening blocks drainage and fills the middle ear with fluid. Patients may also report epistaxis or blood stained postnasal discharge with **nasal obstruction**. Skull base invasion produces **cranial neuropathies**, with the abducens nerve failing first and causing double vision, followed by trigeminal pain or numbness and later cranial nerve signs. The classic **Trotter triad** combines conductive deafness, neuralgic facial pain, and ipsilateral palatal immobility. Suspected cases need nasendoscopy with biopsy of any fossa lesion.
steps.say: A middle ear full of fluid on one side in an adult should always raise suspicion of a nasopharyngeal growth. The tumour blocks the Eustachian tube and traps fluid behind the eardrum. Bleeding from the nose or blood mixed with postnasal discharge adds further warning. When the skull base gets invaded, the sixth cranial nerve fails first and produces double vision. Doctors confirm the diagnosis by passing an endoscope through the nose and sampling any suspicious tissue.

steps.tx: Magnetic resonance imaging of the nasopharynx and skull base defines soft tissue extent and perineural spread, while computed tomography shows bone erosion. Plasma **EBV DNA** supports screening in endemic programmes and helps track prognosis during follow up. Audiometry documents hearing loss, and staging **PET CT** maps advanced nodal and distant disease. **Radiotherapy** is the primary treatment because the site is surgically inaccessible, with concurrent chemotherapy added for locoregionally advanced tumours, and modern intensity modulated plans spare the parotids and brain.
steps.say: Magnetic resonance imaging shows the soft tissue extent best, and computed tomography reveals bone erosion at the skull base. A blood test for viral DNA helps with screening and with tracking the disease over time. Hearing testing records any loss from tube blockage, and a whole body scan maps distant spread in advanced cases. Radiation forms the main treatment because surgeons cannot safely reach this site. Chemotherapy joins radiation when the disease has spread through the neck nodes.

steps.tx: The paired scans display an enhancing central **primary mass** with arrows that mark upward **skull base invasion** and bilateral **metastatic nodes**. This matches the workup step where MRI defines soft tissue and perineural extent while CT maps bone erosion. In the exam, link skull base spread with sixth nerve palsy and node disease with the need for concurrent chemotherapy alongside **radiotherapy** in advanced tumours.
steps.say: These paired scans present a bright central mass with arrows that mark skull base invasion above and diseased nodes below. The picture confirms why magnetic resonance imaging remains the best test for soft tissue and perineural spread. Skull base invasion explains the sixth nerve palsy that causes double vision. Nodal spread explains why doctors add chemotherapy to radiation in advanced disease.

steps.tx: **Adenoid hypertrophy** troubles children but is rare in adults, where regrowth demands exclusion of lymphoma or immune deficiency. A **Thornwaldt cyst** is a midline remnant of the notochord that stays silent unless infection brings halitosis and discharge. Juvenile angiofibroma can extend upward, and inverted papilloma or lymphoma may mimic cancer closely. Any adult nasopharyngeal mass with nodes follows the malignancy pathway until **histology** decides, and even a unilateral effusion without a visible mass still needs endoscopy and imaging follow up.
steps.say: Enlarged adenoids are common in children, but fresh growth in an adult needs a search for lymphoma or immune deficiency. A midline cyst from leftover embryonic tissue usually stays quiet unless infection sets in. Some benign tumours of youth and inverted growths can look exactly like cancer on first inspection. Any adult lump in this region with neck nodes travels the cancer pathway until tissue sampling gives the answer. Even fluid behind one eardrum without a visible mass deserves endoscopy and imaging follow up.
